dsmPointer: See DSM-5-TR: Bipolar and Related Disorders — Bipolar I Disorder
summary: A recurrent mood condition defined by at least one full high: days of unusually high, overconfident or irritable mood with surging energy, little need for sleep, racing ideas, grand plans and risky choices, often severe enough to bring hospital care, police contact or a break with reality. Most people also have depressive episodes, and these usually take up more of their lives than the highs. Clients often seek help when low and may describe the highs as their best times, so ask about them directly and, with consent, ask someone close. Treatment centers on medication from a prescriber, with psychoeducation, regular routines and early-warning plans alongside. For clinician review only; this is not a diagnosis.

durationGate.note: Ask how many days the high lasted, whether it was present most of each day, and whether it led to hospital care. Check the duration and severity thresholds in DSM-5-TR.

ruleOuts.label: Stimulants, steroids and other substances or medicines
ruleOuts.note: Cocaine, amphetamines, high-dose corticosteroids and some antidepressant starts can bring on manic-like states. Review the medication list with the prescriber. This app does not store substance-use information.

ruleOuts.label: Thyroid, neurological and other medical causes
ruleOuts.note: Hyperthyroidism, brain injury, seizures, multiple sclerosis, dementia and some infections can cause elation, irritability or disinhibition, especially with a first episode after age 40. Arrange a medical work-up.

ruleOuts.label: Primary psychotic disorder
ruleOuts.note: Hallucinations or delusions that persist when mood is level point toward a schizophrenia-spectrum or schizoaffective picture.

ruleOuts.label: Unipolar depression without a history of highs
ruleOuts.note: Ask the client and, with consent, someone who knows them well about past periods of unusual energy, little sleep or risky spending; highs are often missed or remembered as good spells.

specifiers.label: Current episode: manic, depressed, mixed or in remission (descriptive)
specifiers.note: The current state sets the ICD-10-CM code (F31.1x to F31.7x). See DSM-5-TR for episode specifiers.

specifiers.label: Psychotic features (descriptive)
specifiers.note: Code with psychotic features (F31.2, F31.5, F31.64) when present; arrange an urgent psychiatric evaluation.

differentials.label: Bipolar II disorder
differentials.distinguishing: Highs are milder and shorter, never lead to hospital care or psychosis, and depressive episodes dominate.

differentials.label: Major depressive disorder
differentials.distinguishing: No history of highs. Ask about past highs at every assessment of depression.

differentials.label: Substance-induced mood changes
differentials.distinguishing: Highs only during stimulant use or steroid treatment and clearing with abstinence.

differentials.label: Schizoaffective disorder
differentials.distinguishing: Psychotic symptoms continue for weeks when mood is level.

differentials.label: Borderline personality pattern
differentials.distinguishing: Mood shifts last hours rather than days, follow interpersonal triggers, and come without a sustained drop in need for sleep.

comorbidities.label: Depressive episodes
comorbidities.note: Depressive episodes in bipolar I need different treatment; antidepressant use alone can destabilize mood. Coordinate with the prescriber.

comorbidities.label: Alcohol use disorder
comorbidities.note: Common alongside bipolar disorder and linked to more episodes; screen for it.

comorbidities.label: Adult ADHD
comorbidities.note: Distractibility and restlessness overlap; ADHD is lifelong and steady, mood highs come in episodes.

comorbidities.label: Anxiety disorders
comorbidities.note: Anxiety is common and is linked to a harder course; screen with the GAD-7.

interventions.name: Referral for medication evaluation (first line)
interventions.evidence: NICE CG185 recommends a mood stabilizer or antipsychotic, prescribed and monitored by a specialist, as the core of treatment.
interventions.note: Refer to psychiatry or a psychiatric nurse practitioner; urgent referral during a high, with psychosis or with risk.

interventions.name: Psychoeducation (adjunct)
interventions.evidence: Group psychoeducation cut recurrences in a randomized trial (Colom et al., 2003).
interventions.note: Teach early warning signs, the role of sleep and routine, and medication questions to bring to the prescriber.

interventions.name: Interpersonal and social rhythm therapy (adjunct)
interventions.evidence: Frank et al. (2005) found IPSRT during acute treatment linked to longer time well.
interventions.note: Steady daily rhythms (wake time, meals, activity) and interpersonal problem work.

interventions.name: Family-focused therapy and intensive psychotherapy (adjunct)
interventions.evidence: In STEP-BD, intensive psychotherapy (family-focused, IPSRT or CBT) sped recovery from bipolar depression compared with brief care (Miklowitz et al., 2007).
interventions.note: Involve family, with consent, in communication and relapse planning.

interventions.name: Safety planning
interventions.evidence: Suicide risk is raised in bipolar disorder, especially in depressive and mixed states.
interventions.note: Build a safety plan and discuss lethal means; this app never rates risk.

culturalNotes: Expressions of energy, religiosity and confidence differ across cultures. Judge a change against the client's own usual self and community norms, not the clinician's.
Black and Latino clients with mood symptoms are more often misdiagnosed with psychotic disorders in US studies. Take a careful mood history before concluding that psychosis is primary.
Shame about psychiatric illness and medication can delay care. Explain that mood episodes are common, treatable and not a character flaw, and ask what the family believes about the cause.
Night shifts, travel across time zones, fasting periods and late-night celebrations can disrupt sleep and routine. Plan around them with the client rather than asking them to give them up.
Use a trained professional interpreter, not family members, and check that key terms translate with the meaning you intend.
If the client wants faith or spiritual practice included, follow their lead and get informed consent first (see the AACC Code of Ethics for faith-based counselors); never impose beliefs.

redFlagRules.message: Suicidal thoughts or self-harm are documented in this input. Ask directly about intent, plan and access to means, follow your crisis protocol and build a safety plan with the client; this app never rates risk.
Psychotic symptoms are documented alongside the mood picture. Psychosis during a high or low is a medical priority: arrange an urgent psychiatric evaluation and check safety at home.
